A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FakeVLM/FakeClue work, with matching architecture, contributions, and experiments. Text, equations, tables, and figures are readable. V1 ends with references; v2 includes Appendices A–H, allowing reliable comparison of the supplied material.

before.justification: Sections 5.3–5.5 report original FakeVLM detection, artifact-explanation, and ablation results on FakeClue, LOKI, DMimage, DD-VQA, and FF++.

after.justification: V2 retains the original experimental results and additionally reports distortion robustness and category-level performance in Appendices C–D.

M1.justification: The architecture, loss, full fine-tuning, and explanatory VQA procedure remain unchanged. However, Section 3.2 changes the stated annotation-prompt count from 12 to 14. Since v1 already covers seven categories and illustrates a face prompt but lacks the full templates, the PDFs do not establish whether this reflects a procedural change or corrected documentation.

E1.justification: The named benchmarks and detection/explanation tasks are retained. Appendix C adds testing on compressed, resized, noisy, and otherwise transformed FakeClue images, extending input conditions. Appendix D disaggregates existing LOKI coverage rather than establishing a newly added domain.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds CNNSpot, FreqNet, Fatformer, UnivFD, AIDE, and NPR to the FakeClue/LOKI comparison; CNNSpot and UnivFD previously appeared only in the DMimage comparison. New Table 8 substantially broadens LOKI comparators, including MiniCPM-V-2.6, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, and Gemini-1.5-Pro.

E3.justification: Section 4.3 revises the stated learning rate from 2e-4 to 2e-5, retaining two epochs, eight A100 GPUs, and batch size 32 per GPU. Appendix C introduces specified distortion settings, including JPEG qualities, resizing scales, and Gaussian-noise variances. The learning-rate revision does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendices C–D add systematic robustness testing across twelve perturbation conditions and category-level generalization analysis. Appendix B supplies benchmark-separated training-strategy results. The existing explanatory-text ablation is retained; the dedicated DD-VQA explanation examples in v1 Figure 6 are removed, while the real-image case figure gains another example.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests for its experiments. The additional results retain point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: V2 adds expert-baseline, perturbation, and category results in Tables 2 and 7–8, including 89.5% FakeClue accuracy under Blur3 versus 98.6% on original images. Table 3 changes Gram-Net's real-image Acc/F1 from 22.8/34.1 to 62.8/54.1. Existing main-table FakeVLM scores are retained; conversion from decimals to percentages is not a performance change.

T1.justification: The encoder, projector, and training-objective equations are unchanged. Equation 1 makes the candidate-caption set and aggregation prompt explicit but restates the existing aggregation operation. Neither version provides theoretical propositions or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same contributions: general synthetic-image and DeepFake detection with explanations, expert-comparable performance without an additional classifier, and a seven-category FakeClue dataset exceeding 100,000 images. Additional evidence does not materially redefine these claims.

C2.justification: V2 introduces substantive limitations absent from v1: inherited annotation-model biases, missed fine-grained artifacts, and reduced sensitivity to high-fidelity synthetic images (Appendix F). It adds interpretations concerning alignment with human artifact perception and category-dependent performance, plus discussion of deployment errors and computational-access limitations in Appendix G.

D1.justification: Appendix H supplies seven real/fake prompt pairs and aggregation instructions previously unavailable in v1. V2 also explicitly identifies Qwen2-VL as aggregator, specifies the GPT-4o snapshot, and marks FakeClue-trained expert baselines. The abstract changes a promised code/data release to reported availability of code, model weights, and data; external availability was not verified.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations including LEGION, GPT-ImgEval, newer LMM-efficiency and geospatial work, and newly compared detectors. FWA and CDFA citations now identify detection papers instead of unrelated works. These are localized reference and contextual updates; the central positioning against generic LMMs and tampering-focused systems remains unchanged.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and contribution narrative are retained. V2 condenses several dataset, training, and results paragraphs, clarifies aggregation terminology, renames the DeepFake category to face manipulation, updates affiliation text, and adds appendix cross-references and acknowledgments.

P2.justification: V2 changes the two-column layout to a single-column conference format, expands Table 2, and adds Tables 7–8. It relocates retained figures, removes the introductory and dedicated DD-VQA case figures, and adds a dataset gallery, benchmark-separated training chart, and radar summary. The real-image figure expands from two examples to three.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses substantial reproducibility and validation gaps by supplying annotation prompts and robustness results only referenced in v1, adding expert comparisons on the primary benchmarks, and documenting annotation bias and high-fidelity failure cases. These gains outweigh the loss of dedicated DD-VQA explanation examples. Reporting remains imperfect: some LOKI baseline scores differ between Tables 2 and 8 without a clarified setting difference.
